column2: Why does anterior cerebral infarction cause leg-predominant weakness, whereas middle cerebral infarction causes face-arm-predominant deficit?

column2: How is the visual field mapped onto primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus?
column3: Central vision lies posteriorly and peripheral fields more anteriorly; the superior visual field is represented below the sulcus and the inferior field above it.

column2: How are corticobulbar, corticospinal, visual and auditory fibres arranged in the internal capsule?

column2: Why can a small deep infarct cause a dense contralateral deficit without aphasia, neglect or seizures?
column3: Projection fibres are tightly packed in the internal capsule, so a small lesion interrupts many of them while sparing cortex.

column2: How does cerebral venous thrombosis differ from arterial occlusion in mechanism and course?

column2: Which structures can uncal herniation compress, and why does intracranial mass eventually cause herniation?
